name: Jamal Ito

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I work for the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I buy for Ridgeway Farm and Feed, a supplier to farms across three valleys. That's feed, fertiliser, fencing, seed and veterinary supplies. I walk the yard at six before the first farmers come in, then I sit down with the price lists and ring the mills and the seed companies. The farmers trust me because I've told them the truth about a bad batch before it cost them money. Thirty-two years at the same counter and desk.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What part of that day do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: What I like is the farmers. I know their fathers and their grandfathers. What wears me out is how the head office keeps sending new forms and new targets from people who've never seen a cow. My wife Ruth teaches Sunday school and works at the bakery, and we're up before the church bell most mornings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's what I expected. Every few years somebody says machines will change everything. We had computers, we had the internet, and farmers still need feed and I still need to know which mill sells the good stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, my worry isn't machines at all. It's the farm economy. When milk prices fall, my customers cut back, and then Ridgeway cuts back. And my savings are a few weeks' worth, with Ruth's bakery wage the only thing steadier.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am. I'd work, go to church, help my neighbours. I'd keep a little aside, maybe 60 a month, and I'd ask head office to let me keep my old phone-and-ledger way. I wouldn't touch the AI tools. I like to hear a man's voice when he gives me a price.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Settled, but with a tightness underneath. A farm town is only as strong as its farms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the Haverty dairy selling up cost a tenth of sales. How did you and Ruth feel about it that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years ago the Haverty dairy, a customer of 40 years, sold up. We lost a tenth of our sales that quarter. Nobody lost a job, but I did the maths on my own, and it wasn't pretty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a fair market look like for your farmers?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I blame cheap imports and the supermarkets, and a government that makes a farmer fill in forty forms before he can buy a tractor part. They've never worked a day in the field. I'd say free markets are fine, but fair ones.

say: I'd say it's what I **expected**: every few years someone says machines will change everything.
I'd say free markets are fine, but they should be **fair** ones.
think: My worry isn't machines but the **farm economy**: if milk prices fall, Ridgeway cuts back.
My savings are a few weeks' worth, and Ruth's bakery wage is steadier.
do: Carry on working, going to **church** and helping neighbours.
Ask head office to let me keep my **phone-and-ledger** way.
feel: Settled on top, but a **tightness** underneath.
S0.quote: Two years ago the Haverty dairy, a customer of 40 years, sold up. We lost a tenth of our sales that quarter.
fieldNote: Not **worried** about AI, but a falling farm economy and thin savings already weigh on him.
Blames imports, **supermarkets** and government paperwork rather than technology.
Loyal to farmers and **distrusts** head office, so he avoids AI tools.

steps.text: Keep walking the yard and ringing the mills each morning
Put 60 a month into a savings account
Ask head office to keep my phone-and-ledger routine

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's mostly city talk. Buying and booking, maybe, if you've never met your suppliers. For us it's about knowing which man sells good seed and which one is only good at talking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: But I'm not a fool. Head office has already put in a system that suggests orders. If it gets cleverer, they'd say we only need two buyers instead of four. I'm the oldest buyer, so I know where that points.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing the calls and teaching the younger lad, Tobias, what I know. I'd go to the farmers' association meeting and say what I think. I wouldn't learn the software, because I don't trust anything I can't question. And I'd talk to our pastor and my brother about what we'd do if my hours were cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Unsettled. Like seeing a storm over the next valley.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about the fertiliser mistake. What did you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last spring the system suggested a cheap fertiliser that didn't suit our clay soil. I caught it because I'd seen the same mistake in 1998. If I weren't there, a dozen farms would have lost part of a crop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you wouldn't learn the software. Is that a decision or a feeling?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say head office is at fault for rushing. And the politicians who sold the country on cheap everything. People like me, who know the ground, get overruled by a spreadsheet.

say: I'd say the talk is **mostly city talk**: knowing which seller is good matters.
I'd say people who know the ground get **overruled** by a spreadsheet.
think: Head office could say two buyers instead of four, and I'm the **oldest** buyer.
I don't trust anything I can't **question**, so I won't learn the software.
do: Keep doing the calls and teach the younger buyer **Tobias** what I know.
Talk to my pastor and brother about a plan if my **hours** are cut.
feel: **Unsettled**, like seeing a storm over the next valley.
S1.quote: The system suggested a cheap fertiliser that didn't suit our clay soil. I caught it because I'd seen the same mistake in 1998.
fieldNote: Admits the **ordering** system will shrink the buyer team and that he is the oldest.
Refuses AI as a matter of trust, which leaves his only **protection** his local knowledge.
Turns to **community**, church and family before the firm.

steps.text: Teach Tobias how to spot a bad batch of seed
Speak at the farmers' association about head office's system
Ask the pastor and my brother for a plan if hours are cut

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a terrible thing to spring on people, and I'd say it plainly in church and at the feed counter. I'd ask who gave anybody the right to do this without asking the rest of us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'm out inside a year. Ruth and I would be in trouble. We have almost nothing saved, the farms around us are losing customers, and nobody within an hour would hire a man of 60 to do a job a machine does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to the owner, Mr. Lindqvist, and ask him straight what he plans. I'd ask my brother about working at his garage and the church about help. I'd sell the old truck. Then I'd see if the warehouse needs men, since robots aren't coming for three years more. And I'd give Ruth every hour she needs at the bakery.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hard. Plain hard. I'd pray on it, and I'd still lie awake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said family is what's left when a job goes. What would you ask of them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my son Daniel he should stay in his trade as a mechanic and not count on me. And I'd tell my daughter to keep her teaching job. Family is what's left when a job goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you think should have been asked before this was done?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd blame the people who built it and the ones who let them. I don't hate the machine. I hate being told it's progress while my neighbours lose their living.

say: I'd call it a terrible thing to spring on people and ask who gave anyone the **right**.
I'd say it plainly in **church** and at the feed counter.
think: I think I'm **out inside a year**, and nobody within an hour would hire a man of 60.
We have almost nothing saved, and the farms around us are losing customers.
do: Ask the owner, Mr. Lindqvist, straight out what he **plans**.
Ask my brother about work at his **garage** and the church about help.
Sell the **old truck** and look for warehouse work.
feel: **Hard**, plain hard: I'd pray, and still lie awake.
S2.quote: I don't hate the machine. I hate being told it's progress while my neighbours lose their living.
fieldNote: **Expects** to lose his job within a year with no savings and few local jobs, so alarmed.
Turns to faith, brother and church for support, and to the **warehouse** as his fallback.
Anger is aimed at **builders** and enablers of AI, not the machine itself.

steps.text: Ask Mr. Lindqvist for his plan for the buyers
Ask my brother about shifts at his garage
Ask the church for help with the bills
Sell the old truck for the cash

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a bit of mercy. It's enough time to see which way the wind blows. I'd tell the young ones to go and learn a trade they can do with their hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be 63. I think I could scrape through to 65 and then take a small pension, if head office keeps me. It's not safe, but it's possible. I'd hate to be pushed out before then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work and save as much as I can, about 150 a month, by cutting out the weekend trips to see the grandchildren. I'd tell Daniel to train his own apprentice and make a family business of his garage work. I'd go to the association and ask them to push the government for pension protection. And I'd still refuse the new software, but I'd show Tobias the real knowledge, so one of us stays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tense, but with a bit of breathing room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said cutting trips to see the grandchildren hurts. What else would you give up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ruth wants to keep the grandchildren close, so cutting trips hurts. We'd try to drive on Sundays only. It's a small thing but it hurts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a proper send-off look like to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the firm cut me at 63, I'd feel betrayed. I've given it thirty-odd years. I'd want a proper send-off, a pension bridge and a thank-you that means something.

say: I'd say five years is a bit of **mercy**, enough to see which way the wind blows.
I'd tell the young ones to learn a **trade** with their hands.
think: At 63 I could scrape to **65** and a small pension if head office keeps me.
Being pushed out before then would feel like **betrayal**.
do: Save **150 a month** by cutting weekend trips to see the grandchildren.
Ask the association to push the government on **pension protection**.
Show Tobias the **real knowledge** so one of us stays.
feel: **Tense**, but with a little breathing room.
S3.quote: I'd tell the young ones to go and learn a trade they can do with their hands.
fieldNote: Five years brings a **believable** path to 65, but the pension is small and the firm has no loyalty to him.
Refuses AI still, putting faith in passing **knowledge** to Tobias.
Cutting **grandchildren** visits shows the human cost of thin savings.

steps.text: Save 150 a month by dropping the weekend trips
Press the association to lobby for pension protection
Show Tobias how to judge a mill and a seed lot
Ask the firm for a pension bridge if it cuts me at 63

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, I'd say that's a different story. I'd tell people it gives a family time to put a plan together, to teach the young ones real work, and not to fall for easy promises.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be 68 and retired, so honestly it doesn't touch me directly. It's my children I think about, and their children. I'd feel more relaxed, but the savings are small, so I'd still watch the pennies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work to 65 as planned. I'd help Daniel set up his own garage business, since a trade is a good defence. I'd tithe what I can to the church and keep giving to the food pantry. And I'd vote for the people who say work, family and apprenticeships come first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Peaceful, mostly. It's the first one where I think my family comes through fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd watch the pennies even then. What would worry you most about money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What I'd worry about is that the thinking jobs go first and the hands-on jobs last. My daughter is a teacher, and I can't say how safe that is. Maybe she'd need to learn a trade too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why apprenticeships and not handouts?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want the government to back apprenticeships and not hand out money for nothing. A man should be given a chance to work for his keep.

say: I'd tell people a decade gives a family time to teach the young **real work**.
I'd say don't fall for **easy promises**.
think: At 68 I'd be **retired**, so it doesn't touch me directly; my children are what I think about.
My savings are small, so I'd still watch the **pennies**.
do: Help my son Daniel set up his own **garage business**.
Vote for people who put work, family and **apprenticeships** first.
feel: **Peaceful**, mostly: the first world where my family comes through fine.
S4.quote: A man should be given a chance to work for his keep.
fieldNote: **Retirement** falls in the window, so his job isn't at risk, but thin savings stay on his mind.
Supports **apprenticeships** and work over handouts, consistent with his traditional outlook.
His focus is family and **community** more than himself.

steps.text: Help Daniel set up his own garage business
Vote for candidates who back apprenticeships
Keep giving to the church food pantry each month

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one. Two years, no savings, and a firm that doesn't ask. What would help is honest talk from the owner, a pension that doesn't punish an older man for losing his job, and a chance to do honest work somewhere. I'm not asking for a handout. I'm asking for a fair chance.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that people like me aren't against progress. We just want it done with some respect for the ones who built the place. And I'd like a sign somebody remembers my name.

headlineQuote: I'm not asking for a handout. I'm asking for a fair chance.
portrait: **Jamal Ito**, 58, buys feed, seed and fertiliser for a farm supplier, with 32 years at the same desk.
He is **traditional** and resistant: he trusts voices over screens, never uses AI and distrusts head office.
Thin savings, a falling farm economy and few jobs nearby keep him **anxious** in every world but the ten-year one.
He turns to **family**, **church** and the farmers' association before the firm.
He wants apprenticeships, work and a fair chance, not handouts.
biggestWorry: The **2028** world, because two years with no savings gives him no fair chance.
whatWouldHelp: Honest talk from the owner, a **pension** that doesn't punish an older man for job loss, and honest work to move to.
Some **respect** for the people who built the place.
